paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A desert refers to a barren section of land, mainly in arid and semi-arid areas, where there is almost no precipitation, and the environment is hostile to life. Deserts have been classified in a number of ways, generally combining total precipitation, the number of days on which rain falls, temperature, humidity, and sometimes additional factors. In some places, deserts have clear boundaries marked by rivers, mountains or other landforms, while in other places, there are no clear-cut borders between desert and other landscapes.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In arid areas where there is no vegetation cover protecting the land, sand and dust storms will frequently take place. This phenomenon often occurs at desert margins instead of within the deserts, where there are already no finer materials left. When a steady wind starts to blow, fine particles on the open ground will begin vibrating. As the wind picks up, some of the particles are lifted into the air. When they fall onto the ground, they hit other particles which will then be jerked into the air in their turn, initiating a chain reaction.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There has been a great deal of publicity about how severe desertification can be, but the academic community has never agreed on the causes of desertification. A common misunderstanding is that a shortage of precipitation causes desertification—even the land in some barren areas will soon recover after the rain falls. In fact, more often than not, human activities are responsible for desertification. It might be true that the explosion in world population, especially in developing countries, is the primary cause of soil degradation and desertification. Since the population density has increased, cultivation has expanded into progressively drier areas. These regions are especially prone to periods of severe drought, which explains why crop failures are common. Growing most crops requires the natural vegetation cover to be removed first; when crop failures occur, extensive tracts of land are devoid of plant cover and thus susceptible to wind and water erosion. Throughout the 1990s, dryland areas went through a population growth of 18.5 per cent, mostly in severely impoverished developing countries.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Raising livestock in semi-arid areas accelerates soil erosion and is one cause of advancing desertification. In such areas where the vegetation is dominated by grasses, livestock grazing is a major economic activity. Grasses are necessary for anchoring vulnerable topsoil in a dryland area. When a specific field is used to graze an excessively large herd, the field will lose vegetation cover, and the soil will be trampled and pulverised, leaving the topsoil exposed to destructive forces such as wind and sudden thunderstorms. For centuries, nomads have moved their flocks and herds wherever pasture can be found, and oases have offered opportunities for a more settled way of living. For some nomads, wherever they move to, the desert follows.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Trees are of great importance when it comes to maintaining topsoil and reducing wind speed. In many Asian countries, firewood is the chief fuel used for cooking and heating, which has caused uncontrolled clear-cutting of forests in dryland ecosystems. When too many trees are cut down, windstorms and dust storms tend to occur.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Political conflicts and wars can also contribute to desertification. To escape invading enemies, refugees may move en masse into some of the planet’s most vulnerable ecosystems. They may bring farming practices that are unsuited to their new environment.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In the 20th century, one US state had a large section of farmland that had turned into desert. Since then, measures have been implemented to prevent desertification from recurring. People are encouraged to find livelihoods that place fewer demands on local land and natural resources but can still generate a viable income. Such livelihoods include but are not limited to dryland aquaculture for raising fish and crustaceans and producing industrial compounds derived from microalgae, greenhouse agriculture, and tourism-related activities. Another way to prevent the recurrence of desertification is to improve the economic prospects in city centres and places outside of drylands. Changing the general economic and institutional structures that create new opportunities for people to support themselves would alleviate the current pressures accompanying the desertification processes.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Today, new technologies are being used to address the problems caused by desertification. Satellites have been used to investigate the influence that people and livestock have on desertification. Even so, alternative technologies are still needed to address the problems and processes of desertification.
